newsitem.title: NORWAY: Analyst sees aluminium prices rising modestly.
newsitem.headline: Analyst sees aluminium prices rising modestly.

text.p: Prices for aluminium are likely to recover from current lows but will see only modest increases over the next two years, an industry analyst said on Thursday.
John Martin, research manager at London-based CRU International, said he expected growth in consumption to slightly outpace new capacity over the next ten years.
"The market is oversold at today's level so we expect a recovery from these lows," Martin told a seminar in Oslo.

"But we see only modest increases in 1997 and 1998, which could lead to a cancellation of some smelter projects. This could in turn produce a deficit in supply and therefore a rise in prices around 1999 or 2000."

Aluminium, used mainly in transport, packaging and construction, slumped on Monday to a 2-1/4 year low of $1,414 a tonne on the London Metal Exchange (LME). Prices have since edged up slightly to between $1,420-1,425 a tonne on Thursday.
Martin forecast an average aluminium price of $1,650 a tonne between 1996 and 2005.

Of the metal's three main markets, Martin said transport was projected to grow at the fastest rate of around three percent per year up to 2005 with gains in market share in engine blocks, cyclinder heads and suspension parts, radiators and wheels.
But consumption in packaging would likely be restrained by substitution and he predicted an annual growth rate of 0.5 percent.
"Aluminium in packaging faces significant threats from PET bottles in North America. In fact packaging applications in this market will probably decline," the analyst said.

Modest growth was seen in the building sector in the main markets of North America and Europe, but a decline in Japanese housing would limit shipments there. Demand growth in construction was forecast at about 0.9 percent per year to 2005.

Primary aluminium consumption in the main markets of North American, Japan and Europe was expected to grow at below the three percent per year forecast for global consumption over the ten year period due to a faster growth rate for recycled metal.
Latin America and Asia -- excluding Japan -- would be the star performers with primary growth seen at three percent and 4.5 percent respectively, Martin said.

Primary consumption in the Western world was forecast at 22.2 million tonnes by 2005, an increase of 4.7 million tonnes from 1995 levels. Meanwhile, world smelting capacity was predicted to rise by around 4.6 million tonne by 2005, including some 900,000 tonnes in capacity "creep".

"Generally speaking those regions who already have to import a large amount of their requirements -- Europe, Japan and other Asia -- will see this requirement grow strongly over the forecast period," Martin said.

European import requirement was expected to rise to 2.3 million tonnes in 2005 from 1.4 million tonnes in 1995. Japan's imports would rise about 400,000 tonnes to around 2.8 million tonnes in the 10 year period.
"On the other hand Africa, Latin America and the Middle East are expected to significantly increase their exportable surpluses," he said.
Exports from so-called "East bloc" countries were expected to decrease due to strong growth in demand outpacing growth in production, especially in China and eastern Europe.

"China's import requirement should double to around 500,000 tonnes by 2005," Martin said. "Sluggish growth in CIS primary consumption and a new smelter in Kazakhstan will result in little change in CIS exports over the forecast period."
As a result net exports from the "Eastern bloc" were projected to fall on an annual basis by around 500,000 tonnes to 2005.
--Tanya Pang, Oslo newsroom, +47 22 42 50 41
